contentBlocks.value: (5a − b)² is already a square and 81c² = (9c)²

solutionSteps.instruction: Apply the difference of two squares.
Check for any further common factor.

contentBlocks.value: Neither bracket has a common factor

strategyBlocks.value: Treat 5a − b as a single quantity and 9c as the other square root, then apply a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b).

whyThisWorks.value: Because the rule depends only on having two squares subtracted, the first square may be an entire bracket. Keeping 5a − b together avoids expanding, and the ± 9c is simply attached to each copy of it.

commonErrors.misconception: Expanding (5a − b)² unnecessarily and then losing terms.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Expanding (5a − b)² unnecessarily and then losing terms.

commonErrors.misconception: Giving the square root of 81c² as 9c² instead of 9c.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Giving the square root of 81c² as 9c² instead of 9c.

commonErrors.misconception: Mishandling the signs and writing 5a − (b − 9c) in place of 5a − b − 9c.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Mishandling the signs and writing 5a − (b − 9c) in place of 5a − b − 9c.

examTip.value: When a squared bracket appears, keep it whole — expanding almost always makes the factorisation harder, not easier.
